blocks.x: This tab answers: what the game looks like, why it looks that way, and what it costs to make every asset and level.
Fill 5.1 and 5.2 before any production art is commissioned; they are the contract every asset is reviewed against. Leave 5.8 counts provisional until the vertical slice passes its playtest gate.

Write the visual thesis as one sentence a contractor can repeat without the document. Prove it with three pillars, four references, and a list of what the game must never look like. If two pillars conflict, the thesis decides.

The thesis is a production tool, not a slogan. It names the emotional promise, the material reality, and the rule that resolves arguments. Give it to an artist new to the project and ask for a prop sketch. If the sketch could belong to three games, the thesis is too vague.
Visual thesis: {{A working lunar outpost should look like a toy set a child assembled on the kitchen table: chunky, warm, repairable, and lit by a sun that never quite sets.}}
A base you could hold in one hand: chunky toys, warm light, and every machine wearing its status on its face.

x: **Readable first.** Every asset must be identifiable by silhouette at thumbnail size and in grayscale; detail only confirms what the shape already said.
**Warm ground, cool air.** Warm albedo and key light on surfaces, cool ambient and sky fill in shadows; this split carries mood without post-processing.
**Handmade, not sloppy.** Chamfers, slight rotations, and visible fasteners suggest care; broken symmetry and dirt suggest neglect. Never confuse the two.

blocks.x: Set a target on four axes so the team argues about the right things. Proportion can be toy-like while materials stay physically plausible; lighting can be stylized while shadow direction stays consistent. Write the target as a range with a reference frame, not as "stylized".

x: **Proportion:** {{1:4 head-to-body for characters; doors 20 percent taller than realistic so avatars read at distance.}}
**Material:** {{flat base colour, roughness 0.8–0.9, metal only where the player must notice it.}}
**Lighting:** {{one warm key, one cool fill, baked bounce; no more than two shadow-casting lights in a gameplay space.}}
**Detail:** {{one hero detail per asset, three secondary details, zero micro-greebles below 2 cm at gameplay distance.}}
Build every prop from three primitive volumes or fewer; if it needs five to read, redesign it.
Give each gameplay category a dominant shape: {{cylinders for resources, boxes for buildings, spheres for characters and pickups}}.
Reserve sharp angles for danger and round curves for safety; the player learns this without a tutorial.
Test silhouettes as pure black shapes on white at 64 px, then at gameplay camera distance.
Keep the top third of every character and interactable clear; the camera and UI live there.

blocks.x: What the game must never look like

x: Photoreal lunar grey: no desaturated regolith, no archival colour grading, no lens flares instead of lighting.
Asset-store collage: no mixed texel density, no competing outline styles, no props from different eras.
Dark for drama: gameplay spaces never drop below {{18 percent}} average luminance.
Detail as realism: no screws, cables, or labels that cannot be read at gameplay distance.
Symmetry as default: perfect mirror layouts read as unbuilt CAD, not as a place someone works.

blocks.label: RULE
blocks.x: Art direction is a constraint system, not a mood board. Every reference must answer a production question: what shape, what colour, what cost, what never.
Define colour by role and lighting by function, then let the palette carry the mood. A palette that exists only as swatches will drift; one tied to gameplay meaning survives outsourcing.
Limit the game to six colour roles. Each role gets one hue family, a value range, and a meaning the player can learn. Decorative colours are the exception, not the base.

x: One warm key per gameplay space at {{15–30 degrees}} elevation; shadows fall away from the camera, never across the play surface.
One cool fill at {{0.2–0.4}} of key intensity; it keeps shadow detail, not a second mood.
Bake static bounce into lightmaps; use real-time lights only for characters, projectiles, and state changes.
Emissive materials are status, not decoration: {{no surface larger than a fist}} glows, and every glow colour has one meaning.
Night and interior scenes raise ambient before lamps; keep walkable edges readable.

head: State
Key and fill
Application
Cost
rows: Warm key, cool sky fill, long shadows
Lower key, amber practicals, blue ambient
Diffuse key, reduced contrast, particle haze
Moonlit cool key, warm interior pools

x: Default camera: {{35–45 degree}} pitch, {{40–50 degree}} vertical FOV, distance set so a two-tile prop fills one third of the screen.
Keep the player on the lower third intersection; the top third belongs to the next decision.
Never move the camera during input unless the player initiated it; forced moves are for deaths, doors, and cutscenes.
Cutscenes use the same lens family; an 18 mm shot reads as a different game.
Test every framing at {{16:9, 21:9, and 4:3}}; UI safe areas are art direction, not a later fix.

blocks.x: Mood wants contrast, atmosphere, and detail; readability wants flat values, clear edges, and one focal point. Resolve the conflict with hierarchy: gameplay-critical shapes keep the highest local contrast, atmosphere stays in the background, and detail lives where the player is not required to act. Squint at every screenshot, then desaturate it. If the interactable disappears, the mood pass has gone too far.
Brief every character on one page and every environment as a kit, not a painting. Characters sell the fantasy; kits decide whether the game ships on time.
A character brief is a contract between design, art, and animation. Fill every row before modelling; a missing row becomes a redesign after rigging.

x: Modular first: one wall, floor, door, corner, and roof must build {{80 percent}} of a room before a hero asset is approved.
Grid discipline: every piece snaps to {{2 m}} and shares one origin convention; a prop that cannot be placed in one drag is a bug.
Landmarks every {{30–45 seconds}}: a tower, a colour break, or a silhouette the player can name. Landmarks are navigation, not decoration.
Traversal readability: walkable edges get a {{15 percent}} value step; climbable surfaces get a unique material; blocked paths never share a colour with open ones.
Dress in layers: structure, function, story, clutter; stop where the camera stops resolving.
One hero asset per zone may break the kit; two means the kit is wrong.

blocks.x: If the game has factions, give each a shape, palette, material, and a tell readable before combat or dialogue.
Build the icon grid and type scale before drawing a single icon. UI art fails when every screen invents its own spacing, stroke, and state colours.

x: Draw on a {{24 px}} grid with a {{2 px}} stroke at 1x; at 4K the icon is scaled, not redrawn.
Keep {{2 px}} padding inside the grid; icons that touch the edge look larger than their neighbours.
Use one corner radius, {{1 px}} at 1x, and one cap style across the set.
Filled shapes carry state, outlines carry category; never mix both without a reason.
Ship SVG source plus PNG at 1x and 2x; the engine imports the raster, the source stays editable.

blocks.x: Pair one display face with one text face at most. If the display face cannot set numbers cleanly, add a tabular numeric face instead of changing the whole UI.

x: Export at {{1x, 2x, 3x}} with power-of-two atlases; pack by screen, not by icon set.
Use 9-slice for panels and buttons; a stretched border makes a UI look amateur.
Define colour, spacing, radius, and type as tokens; screens reference tokens, never hex values.
Ship dark and light from the same tokens; test {{4.5:1}} for body text and {{3:1}} for large text and icons.
Never use pure black or white as a surface; the highest contrast belongs to the one action you want taken.

blocks.x: Budget animation by category and count before blocking a single pose. Animation is the most common place for a small team to promise forty sets and ship twelve.

x: Every action reads in three poses: anticipation, contact, recovery. If the contact pose is not legible as a still, it will not read in motion.
Hold contact for {{2–4 frames}}; the eye needs a beat to register impact.
Open the cancel window at {{60 percent}} of recovery for movement, {{80 percent}} for defence; never cancel anticipation.
Buffer input {{100–150 ms}} before the window opens; players press early, not late.
Keep root motion and the gameplay capsule in sync; if the animation moves the character, the code must know first.
Silhouette first: an effect must read in one frame at gameplay distance, before colour is processed.
One effect, one colour role: damage urgent, healing good, buff attention; never reuse a colour for two meanings.
Cap screen coverage at {{25 percent}} per effect; if it hides the floor, it hides the fight.
Telegraphs last at least {{0.4 s}} and never share a shape with the effect they warn about.
Particle counts are a budget: {{200}} per gameplay effect, {{800}} for a hero moment, {{3}} overlapping systems maximum.

blocks.x: Assign a cost to every animation and effect before it enters the build. Measure at the target camera distance, not a test scene. A character with {{120}} bones and four blend layers costs more than a crowd of props; a full-screen effect costs more than either. Put the numbers in the budget table and review them every milestone.
Count assets by category, then lock the pipeline on one hero asset before the team scales. A pipeline that has not shipped one asset end to end is a hypothesis.

x: Blockout: prove scale, silhouette, and pivot in engine with grey materials.
High poly: add the hero detail and bevel language; no surface noise.
Low poly: retopologize to budget, keep the silhouette, bake once.
UV and texture: one trim sheet or atlas per category; check texel density at gameplay distance.
Import and validate: naming, scale, collision, LODs, and material count pass an automated scene test.
Art pass: lighting, decals, and dressing signed off in the target level, not a viewer.
LOD0 at {{100 percent}} triangles, LOD1 at {{40 percent}}, LOD2 at {{15 percent}}, plus an impostor beyond {{60 m}}.
Textures: {{2K}} for hero characters, {{1K}} for props, {{512}} for dressing, shared trim sheets for kits.
One material per prop unless it changes state; every extra material is a draw call and a variant.
Author collision for anything the player stands on; generated convex hulls are for clutter only.
One-page brief with silhouette, palette, tri and texture budget, and review camera distance.
Engine test scene with the target lighting rig, neighbouring assets, and a capture camera.
Naming, pivot, unit, and export checklist, plus a known-good asset as reference.
Acceptance test in writing: what passes, what gets one revision, what gets rejected.
Two revision rounds included; a third is a new brief and quote.

x: Build one kit per biome or faction, not per level; a kit that serves one room is a hero asset in disguise.
Kit pieces: floor, wall, corner, door, window, stairs, roof, and one damaged variant. Eight build a room; forty build a district.
Set dressing follows function: daily items at hand height, storage high or low, broken things where they fell.
Leave one clear path through every room; clutter on the critical path is a collision bug with a texture.
Reuse kits across levels and rotate {{90, 180, 270 degrees}}; rotation is free variety.

blocks.x: Plan reuse before production. Every kit, rig, animation set, and UI component should have two planned uses; a one-use asset needs a hero justification and a higher review bar. Track reuse in the content matrix so the producer sees the new-to-reused ratio per level. A healthy vertical slice runs on {{60 percent}} reused assets and {{40 percent}} new; a final level should not cost more than the first.
Build the matrix in hours and cost, not in asset counts. Counts hide the work; hours expose it, and the cut list needs hours to be honest.

x: One complete level from title card to results, {{10–15 minutes}} long, with final art on {{70 percent}} of visible assets.
Two characters: the player avatar and one NPC with a full interaction loop.
The core loop playable three times, including one failure and one recovery.
All UI screens the slice touches, in dark and light themes.
One hero VFX moment and one ambient loop, mixed at final loudness.
A build on minimum spec at target frame rate, with telemetry and crash reporting on.
Cut anything absent from the vertical slice or the first {{30 minutes}}.
Cut any asset used once, unless it carries a story beat or a store screenshot.
Cut any system whose failure cannot be explained in one sentence.
Cut any feature needing a new tool, hire, or platform approval inside {{8 weeks}}.
Protect the loop, readability, and frame rate; everything else is negotiable.

blocks.x: Keep a {{20 percent}} schedule buffer and a cut list ranked by cost saved per unit of player value lost. Review it every milestone; a cut list that never changes is a wish list.
Mark this tab done only when a new artist, contractor, and engineer can use it without asking a question.
